newsitem.title: USA: McDonald's rolls out 55-cent campaign at breakfast.
newsitem.headline: McDonald's rolls out 55-cent campaign at breakfast.

text.p: McDonald's Corp. is rolling out its 55-cent promotion at breakfast, a move analysts say will help the fast-food giant test the waters before it discounts its hamburgers.
America's biggest fast-food chain said Wednesday it will offer its four breakfast sandwiches for 55 cents starting Friday.

The sandwiches -- the Egg McMuffin, a product it first introduced in 1972 for 65 cents; Sausage McMuffin with Egg; Bacon, Egg and Cheese Biscuits; and Sausage Biscuit with Egg -- will be priced at 55 cents when customers buy hash browns and a drink.
"McDonald's has a very high market share with breakfast," Ed Rensi, president of the McDonald's USA division, said in a telephone interview.
He added McDonald's serves about one out of every four customers who eat breakfast at a fast-food outlet. "That's 3.4 million customers a day," Rensi said.

The previously announced 55-cent promotion -- called Campaign 55 -- had been expected to begin later in the month, featuring a McDonald's hamburger. The "55" is a reference to 1955, the year the Oak Brook, Ill.-based chain was founded.
Starting with breakfast, however, McDonald's will be able to test consumer response to its price promotion before discounting its hamburgers like the Big Mac and Quarter Pounder, analysts said.
"They'll learn something in the next three or so weeks when this initiative is in place at breakfast and use that to fine-tune the initiative," said Natwest Securities analyst Damon Brundage.

Rensi declined to say how long McDonald's would offer the 55-cent breakfast sandwich promotion, or if it would overlap its expected launch soon of a hamburger discount promotion. But he added this is a "long-term campaign" that will feature different sandwiches over time.
The breakfast promotion also is aimed at boosting McDonald's U.S. sales that, while still dominant in the fast-food industry, have suffered from intense competition, analysts said.

In 1996, McDonald's U.S. same-store sales -- measuring results from units open at least a year -- were down from the prior year. In the first quarter, U.S. same-store sales increased, Rensi said, but he did not say by how much.

McDonald's is hoping Campaign 55 will increase customer traffic at its restaurants, which number more than 21,000 worldwide. It has in excess of 12,000 in the United States alone, about 85 percent of which are owned and operated by franchisees.
The Campaign 55 promotion will be supported by a new national advertising campaign, beginning April 4.
The new commercials, created by Leo Burnett Co. of Chicago, will feature local McDonald's franchisees, managers and restaurant crew. The theme of the advertisements is "My McDonald's."
George Kunz, chairman of the Operators National Advertising Fund, an organisation of McDonald's franchisees, said Campaign 55 was supported by the majority of operators in the chain.
"Ninety percent of the stores voted it in," said Kunz, who owns and operates six McDonald's restaurants in the Las Vegas area.
But some independent franchisees have expressed concerns about whether customer traffic will increase enough to balance the lower promotion prices on some menu items.

Rensi dismissed concerns over profit margins, saying prices will drive increased volume. "The more stuff we sell, the more profit we make," he added. "That's why we've done value for years and years."

In 1991, McDonald's launched Extra Value Meals, which offer a sandwich, French fries and a drink for a set price. McDonald's stock was off 50 cents at $47.75 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
